turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come through. I'll grab a few numbers before the doctor sees you. You look a bit flat.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, well, I've been sitting out there forever. That TV's blaring and I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. Temperature's 37.8. Not sky high. Blood pressure 128 over 78, pulse 92, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): G'day, I'm Dr Shah. Sorry about the wait. What's brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): My right cheek's blown right up, and this tooth's been throbbing like mad. Had a crown put on three days ago.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Mark, her partner. The dentist is away and they reckon they can't fit her till next month. She's been miserable.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I feel like a wet rag. And, well, I've overdone it trying to chew on the other side.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): So, right cheek swelling and a throbbing tooth since the crown, three days, and you're worn out. Which tooth was the crown?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Lower right, at the back. Uh, it throbs all the time, worse if I bite.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any trouble swallowing?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Swallowing's fine. I've just got a frog in my throat, bit croaky since yesterday.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your breathing, any shortness of breath?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's alright. Don't put words in my mouth.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Have you felt feverish at all?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Last night I was hot and shivery. She already said 37.8.
[SEG0016] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She barely slept. And she keeps saying her feet feel dead when she stands up, but she won't mention it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh that's nothing, uh, my feet feel dead, yeah, both of them. Been months, and I dunno when it started. Not why I'm here.

[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll note the numbness and we won't chase it today. Let me look. The right cheek is swollen and tender over the jaw. I can't feel a pocket of pus, and you can open your mouth fully.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): It hurts when you press. Obviously.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you been taking for the pain?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetemol. Two of the 500s, supposed to be four times a day. I've missed a few, I'm all over the shop.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She had some nurofen yesterday, two tablets, then her stomach burned, so she stopped.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. I'll give you a script for amoxacillin, 500 milligrams three times a day for five days. That usually settles a dental infection.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hang on. She can't have penicillin. Years back she got a red rash all over, and they said never again.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Yeah. I forgot about the rash.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks for stopping me. No amoxacillin, and nothing else in the penicillin family. We'll use clindamycin instead, 300 mg by mouth, three times a day, for five days.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Clinda-whatever. Fine, as long as it works. I'm stuffed.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the paracetamol, two 500 milligram tablets up to four times a day, and stay under four grams. Leave the nurofen alone.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, alright.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you get trouble swallowing, or breathing gets hard, or the swelling jumps up towards the eye, go to emergency. Don't wait on me.
[SEG0031] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The dentist really can't see her for weeks. I thought you'd just say wait it out.

[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I did think about pain relief only, and reviewing you in two weeks. With the fever and the cheek like this, I'm not waiting two weeks. I'll book you back here in two days.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days. Great. More waiting rooms.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): We might do a scan of the face if it hasn't settled by then. I'm not booking one today.
[SEG0035] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should she still ring the dentist?
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Ring them tomorrow, tell them there's swelling and a fever. I'll put a short note in for them.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, my throat's just croaky. You're not worried?

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): A croaky voice without trouble swallowing isn't the emergency part. This is most likely a dental infection under that new crown, possibly an early abscess. I can't prove a collection just by looking.
[SEG0039] person_1 (NURSE): No worries. I'll print the script for the chemist and book the two-day review at the desk on your way out.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Take the clindamycin with food if your gut plays up. Anything else you wanted to ask?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Just want the throbbing to stop. And some quiet.
[SEG0042] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll grab the script. Thanks.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Righto. If the breathing changes overnight, don't sit on it, just go in.

spec.situation: Cheek swelling and throbbing toothache for three days after a crown; fever mild; dentist unavailable; doctor prescribes antibiotic, warns about swallowing or breathing difficulty.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
